title: The People Who Rallied to David
overview: This chapter lists the warriors from across Israel who joined David, first a few at a time while he was an outlaw and then in huge numbers when they came to make him king.

parts.label: Saul's own relatives join (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: While David was living as an outlaw at Ziklag, a town the Philistines had let him use, skilled archers and slingers who could fight with either hand joined him, some from Saul's own tribe of Benjamin. The text does not say why they turned from their own kinsman, and some of the place names suggest men from Judah were in this group too.

parts.label: Fierce fighters from Gad (vv. 8-15)
parts.note: Eleven officers from Gad, east of the Jordan River, crossed it in spring when it was in flood and drove off those living in the valleys on both sides. Saying the least was a match for a hundred is most likely an exaggeration praising their courage.

parts.label: David tests the newcomers (vv. 16-18)
parts.note: Having been betrayed before by people he trusted, David warned that he would welcome friends but leave traitors to God's judgment. Amasai, moved by God's Spirit, answered with a pledge of loyalty, and David made these men leaders.

parts.label: Leaders from Manasseh (vv. 19-22)
parts.note: Seven commanders from Manasseh joined David after the Philistine rulers refused to let him march with them against Saul. They helped him fight raiders, and day by day his small band grew into a great army.

parts.label: The tribes gather at Hebron (vv. 23-37)
parts.note: After Saul's death, armed men from every tribe came to Hebron to make David king, though only a few from Benjamin, which had stayed loyal to Saul's family. The numbers are very large, and scholars are unsure whether the word for thousand here sometimes meant a military unit rather than a literal count.

parts.label: A three-day feast (vv. 38-40)
parts.note: United in wanting David as king, the people ate and drank together for three days with food brought from far away. The writer ends on a simple note: there was joy in Israel.

think: When people shift their loyalty from one leader to another, what do you think moves them most: conviction, self-interest, or a sense that the tide has already turned?
